tldr: Addressing harsh, contact-rich construction tasks like high-altitude façade work, this paper presents a semi-autonomous shared control framework that smoothly links VR teleoperation with rule-based autonomy. Real-robot experiments demonstrate both resilience to environmental disturbances and a significant reduction in operator workload.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of the proposed human-in-the-loop system. Operator intent input, decision-making and shared control, and low-level robot execution are layered together, enabling a smooth evolution from full teleoperation to autonomous execution.
overview:
Construction environments—such as exterior façade installation and scaffolding work—are hazardous settings that demand both delicate contact-force control and high-altitude safety. Industrial-style fully autonomous execution (Auto) has long been pursued, but accumulated perception errors caused by site-to-site geometry variations, lighting shifts, and unexpected obstacles often cause autonomous pipelines to fail. On the other hand, full VR teleoperation (TeleOp), where an operator controls everything manually, imposes excessive cognitive and physical burdens during complex dual-arm contact tasks.

To bridge this gap, the authors propose a semi-autonomous shared control (Semi-Auto) paradigm rather than treating teleoperation and autonomy as an all-or-nothing dichotomy. In this setup, human operators handle rough target specification and error recovery, while robot skill primitives take over high-precision, contact-critical actions like fine alignment and drill feed. The paper also introduces the Subtask Allocation Ratio (SAR) as a metric to quantify the degree of human versus robot involvement.

In validation experiments, a setup simulating three realistic tasks—drilling, bracket pick-and-place, and bolt fastening—was tested with 10 novice operators on a real dual-arm platform. Under well-calibrated nominal conditions, rule-based autonomous execution was the fastest and most accurate. However, under severe disturbances (lighting variations, visual occlusions, and physical obstacles), autonomous execution suffered sharp drops in success, whereas semi-autonomous control maintained high success rates thanks to human recovery. Furthermore, operator workload (NASA-TLX) during drilling was reduced by about 46.7% compared with full teleoperation, providing practical design principles for construction robotics.
contributions: Formulated a task-level human-in-the-loop control framework that seamlessly transitions among VR teleoperation, semi-autonomous shared control, and autonomous execution for multi-stage, contact-rich dual-arm construction tasks.
Developed a physical dual-arm robotic system integrating an immersive VR interface with a library of rule-based skill primitives for drilling, bracket placement, and bolt fastening.
Formulated skill-level control weighting and command-priority rules, and introduced the Subtask Allocation Ratio (SAR) metric to quantify the degree of human involvement.

Conducted user studies with 10 novices (100 trials per mode) and disturbance resilience tests, demonstrating that semi-autonomous control substantially aids disturbance recovery and reduces operator workload (by ~46.7%).

sections.heading: The Construction Automation Dilemma and Why We Need Human-in-the-Loop
sections.summary: Labor shortages and safety regulations drive demand for construction robotics, but site uncertainty makes full autonomy brittle and full teleoperation exhausting. This paper proposes a semi-autonomous paradigm that continuously connects both approaches.
sections.details:
The construction industry involves numerous tasks in hazardous, unstructured settings, such as high-altitude façade installation and scaffolding maintenance. While these operations require dexterous bimanual coordination similar to human workers, long shifts significantly heighten worker fatigue and accident risks.

While industrial robots achieve reliable autonomy in structured factory environments, deploying them directly to construction sites is extremely difficult. Variations in site geometry, fluctuating material properties, and sensor noise accumulate errors, causing purely autonomous (Auto) pipelines to quickly get stuck. Conversely, full teleoperation (TeleOp) using VR places an overwhelming cognitive workload on operators, especially during multi-stage contact tasks, which hurts scalability.

Existing shared autonomy research has often lacked control frameworks capable of flexibly handling contact-rich tasks like drilling and bolting, or has treated teleoperation and autonomy as disconnected, mutually exclusive control modes. This is the starting point of the present work. The authors advocate a new control paradigm that smoothly blends high-level human intent transmitted via immersive VR with the autonomous execution of well-defined skill primitives at which robots excel.

sections.heading: At the Intersection of Collaborative Robotics, Dual-Arm Manipulation, and Teleoperation
sections.summary: By reviewing prior work in construction collaboration, dual-arm manipulation, and VR teleoperation, this section highlights the missing link: a mechanism to continuously tune autonomy rather than treating it as an on/off switch.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Human–Robot Collaboration in Uncertain Environments
Research on human–robot collaboration on construction sites has actively explored proximity models, digital twins, and deep reinforcement learning for collision avoidance to ensure worker safety. However, many studies view autonomy as a binary toggle (on/off), lacking the flexibility to dynamically adjust human involvement as task phases progress.

### 2.2 Dual-Arm Manipulation for Contact-Rich Construction Tasks
Dual-arm robots are indispensable for handling and assembling large components. Recently, imitation learning and hierarchical reinforcement learning have increasingly been used to transfer skills from humans to robots. Nevertheless, autonomous control alone remains fragile against unknown disturbances, underscoring the need for a framework where robots maintain low-level stability while interpreting high-level human intent.

### 2.3 Immersive Teleoperation and Shared Autonomy
Teleoperation via VR and digital twins offers intuitive control, but communication latency and operator fatigue are unavoidable. Although shared autonomy approaches that correct human inputs have been proposed to alleviate these issues, methods for dynamically and seamlessly switching the level of autonomy across phases of a multi-stage assembly process have not been well established.

### 2.4 Positioning of This Work
While prior studies focused on single-arm setups or single interfaces, this paper provides novelty by comprehensively integrating VR teleoperation, a physical dual-arm platform, contact-rich façade installation tasks, and the SAR metric to quantify human involvement.

sections.heading: A Three-Layer Paradigm Linking Intent to Contact
sections.summary: This section formulates a three-layer architecture spanning intent, shared actions, and low-level execution, alongside a task decomposition process that blends human and robot authority. The SAR metric is introduced to quantify human involvement.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Hardware Configuration
The experimental platform consists of a Meta Quest 3 VR interface, two FAIRINO 6-DOF collaborative robot arms, and a central workstation. The end-effectors can be equipped with a drill, an electric screwdriver, a suction gripper, and a parallel gripper.

### 3.2.1 Three-Layer Hierarchical Control Architecture
The system is organized into three layers with graduated authority:
- High-level Intent Layer: Led by the human. Decides risk management and the overall task procedure (e.g., align $\rightarrow$ insert $\rightarrow$ fasten).
- Mid-level Action Layer: The core of shared autonomy. Translates human intent into skill primitives such as "align," "grasp," "insert," and "press," blending them with vision and force feedback.
- Low-level Control Layer: Led by the robot. Autonomously guarantees high-frequency (real-time) safety control, including trajectory tracking, hybrid force/position control, and contact state estimation.

### 3.2.2 Three-Step Task Decomposition Process
Execution proceeds through three steps:
1. Task Intent Parsing: Derives the skill sequence and division of responsibility from task goal $\mathbf{T}$ and environmental context $\mathcal{C}$.
2. Skill Selection and Role Allocation: Selects the operational mode (TeleOp / Shared / Auto) for each skill. Human command $u_h$ and robot command $u_r$ are blended using weights $\alpha_i, \beta_i$ defined per skill state (formula: $u(t) = \alpha_i(t) u_h(t) + \beta_i(t) u_r(t)$).
3. Safe Execution in Shared Autonomy: The blended command passes through workspace, velocity, and force/torque safety limiters $\Pi_{\mathrm{safe}}(\cdot)$ before being sent to actuators. When the operator squeezes the VR grip, manual override takes immediate top priority.

### Definition of Subtask Allocation Ratio (SAR)
To evaluate the degree of human involvement, the authors define SAR as the average human control weight across all skill primitives. $\mathrm{SAR} = 0$ corresponds to full autonomy and $\mathrm{SAR} = 1$ to fully manual operation, enabling objective evaluation of autonomy levels.

sections.heading: Applying the Framework to Façade Bracket Installation
sections.summary: Using bracket installation (drilling, placement, bolting) as a representative façade task, this section details task decomposition across three operational modes and the discrete SAR metric.
sections.details:
### (1) Task Decomposition and Workflow
Bracket installation comprises three primary skills: (A) hole drilling, (B) bracket transport and positioning, and (C) bolt fastening. These are demanding tasks requiring dual-arm coordination in confined workspaces and contact force control against the wall surface.

### (2) Skill and Autonomy Allocation
Each skill is assigned to full teleoperation (TeleOp: $\alpha=1, \beta=0$), shared control (Shared: $\alpha \neq 0, \beta \neq 0$), or full autonomy (Auto: $\alpha=0, \beta=1$). Because foundation models like current VLMs or VLAs lack reliability in complex contact operations, the system adopts "Shared" as its baseline strategy: the human handles target identification and coarse approach, while the robot handles fine alignment and force control.

### Quantifying Functional Division via Discrete SAR
By labeling each subtask as human-led ($\delta_i = 1$) or robot-autonomous ($\delta_i = 0$), a discrete SAR is computed as $\mathrm{SAR} = \frac{1}{N} \sum \delta_i$. This provides a clear numerical comparison of how much of a given task is delegated to the robot.

captions.F4: Three-stage workflow of the bracket installation task: (A) pilot hole drilling, (B) bracket grasping and positioning against the wall, and (C) bolt insertion and fastening. Each step is further decomposed into discrete subtasks.

sections.heading: Integrating Vision and Force Control for Autonomous and Teleoperated Pipelines
sections.summary: This section covers implementation details including YOLO-based target recognition, RANSAC wall surface estimation, 6-axis force/torque hybrid control, and intuitive VR controller mapping.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Autonomous Processing Pipeline
- Target Detection: A fine-tuned YOLO26 instance segmentation model (test set mIoU 91.4%) detects marked line intersections and pre-existing holes. To avoid depth noise inside holes, the 3D position is back-projected using the median depth of an annular rim region surrounding the hole mask.
- Wall Plane Estimation: RANSAC extracts the façade plane from point clouds to determine the normal vector (mean normal error $0.61^\circ$, 3D position error $12.4\pm 3.0$ mm).
- Contact Control: Using end-effector 6-axis force/torque sensors, compliance control applies force control along the tool axis and position control along the remaining axes. During autonomous drilling, a constant 30 N feed force is applied; if motor current exceeds 5 A for over 2 seconds, it detects jamming and retracts automatically. Bolt fastening similarly monitors a target depth of 50 mm and tightening torque.

### 5.2 VR Teleoperation Interface
The operator's hand position $\mathbf{p}_h$ and orientation $\mathbf{R}_h$ are mapped in real time to the robot end-effector target pose via a scale factor $s$ and homogeneous transformation matrices. The controller trigger continuously adjusts gripper opening, standard buttons start/stop skills, and a clutch mechanism only tracks motion while the grip button is held.

### 5.3 ROS Safety and Latency
MoveIt continuously checks for collisions, limiting Cartesian velocity to 0.15 m/s during manual control and 0.08 m/s during contact. End-to-end command latency from VR to the robot averages 45 ms, with emergency stop (E-stop) hardware latency at approximately 120 ms.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments: Nominal Performance and Resilience Under Severe Disturbances
sections.summary: Comparative experiments with 10 novices across 100 trials per mode revealed that while autonomy excels in nominal conditions, semi-autonomous control proves essential under disturbances like lighting changes or occlusions, substantially cutting operator workload.
sections.details:
### 6.1 Experimental Setup and Protocol
Ten novice participants evaluated drilling, bracket placement, and bolt fastening across three modes: TeleOp (full teleoperation), Semi-Auto (semi-autonomous), and Auto (fixed rule-based autonomy). Each participant performed 10 trials per mode (100 total trials per mode; Auto was evaluated with 100 autonomous repetitions without an operator).

### 6.2 Three-Mode Comparison in Nominal Conditions
- Drilling: Success rates were 74% for TeleOp, 95% for Semi-Auto, and 100% for Auto. While Auto achieved high perpendicularity precision (error of $0.46^\circ$), Semi-Auto also improved significantly to $1.47^\circ$ compared to TeleOp ($4.79^\circ$).
- Bracket Placement: Involving a large 180-degree arm flip, restricted field-of-view in TeleOp caused success rates to plummet to 12%. In contrast, Semi-Auto reached a 94% success rate (Auto reached 100%).
- Bolt Fastening: Due to the need for dual-arm coordination, TeleOp had only a 5% success rate, whereas Semi-Auto recovered to 88% (Auto reached 98%).
Under well-calibrated nominal conditions, the deterministic Auto mode delivered the highest precision and shortest completion times.

### 6.4 Drilling Robustness Under Severe Environmental Disturbances
The main vulnerability of Auto is its fragility to unexpected environmental changes. To test this, disturbances such as dim lighting, dynamic colored lighting, 25%–75% target occlusion, dropped objects, and arm self-interference were introduced during drilling.
Results diverged sharply: Auto handled minor 25% occlusion, but its success rate dropped to 20%–40% under 50%–75% occlusion or dynamic lighting. In contrast, Semi-Auto maintained high success rates of 70%–90% because operators visually re-identified targets and provided corrections. This demonstrated a clear trade-off: Auto is faster under nominal conditions, but Semi-Auto is indispensable for disturbance recovery on real sites.

### 6.5 Subjective Workload Assessment (NASA-TLX)
NASA-TLX evaluations during drilling showed that overall workload dropped from 61.7 in TeleOp to 32.9 in Semi-Auto—a reduction of approximately 46.7%. Workload decreased consistently across all subscales, including mental demand, physical demand, and frustration.

### 6.6 SAR Sweep Analysis and Failure Modes
When sweeping drilling SAR (human involvement ratio) from 0 to 1, errors and failures spiked when humans took over fine alignment and force control ($\mathrm{SAR} \geq 0.6$). Novice operators struggled with arm orientation adjustments and contact force regulation, proving that delegating these subtasks to the robot is highly effective.

sections.heading: Principles for Adaptive Construction Robotics
sections.summary: This study demonstrates that construction robotics should not treat teleoperation and autonomy as separate worlds, but should adapt human involvement based on task and environmental uncertainty.
sections.details:
This paper presented a human-in-the-loop control paradigm structurally integrating VR-guided teleoperation, shared control, and rule-based autonomy.

The experimental findings are straightforward: while rule-based autonomy delivers top precision and efficiency in calibrated, stable environments, semi-autonomous shared control provides system robustness when real-world construction disturbances—such as lighting shifts, occlusions, and physical interference—occur. Moreover, offloading high-precision contact phases to the robot dramatically cuts operator workload.

Future work includes field testing on actual high-altitude construction sites and expanding the framework toward more sophisticated learning-based autonomous skill acquisition.

takeaways: Instead of choosing strictly between full autonomy and full teleoperation, shared autonomy that tunes human involvement (SAR) per subtask offers a practical solution for unstructured environments.
Delegating fine alignment and contact force control to autonomous robot skills significantly improves novice success rates and cuts operator workload (NASA-TLX) by roughly 46.7%.

Rule-based autonomy excels in calibrated conditions but remains fragile against disturbances like occlusions and lighting shifts, making human cognitive recovery (semi-autonomous intervention) indispensable.
limitations: Experiments were conducted on simulated concrete panels in a laboratory; field validation under actual high-altitude, strong wind, or adverse outdoor weather conditions has not been performed.
Autonomous skills rely on fixed rule sets and pre-trained models, limiting generalization to wall surfaces or structural components with significantly different visual appearances.

Disturbance resilience tests and NASA-TLX workload evaluations were restricted to drilling tasks, leaving disturbance verification for other complex dual-arm tasks (such as bolt fastening) unexplored.
